Review Body:
This little book is well written, and I do not disagree with any of the policies espoused. But there are many, too many examples of Ivy League unawareness of how most people in the U.S. live.

For example, in chapter 16, Snyder advises his readers to “Keep up your friendships abroad, or make new friends in other countries. … Make sure you and your family have passports.” He is a tenured professor at Yale (where I was an undergraduate) and doubtless has colleagues from all over the world. How many Americans can say the same? Passports? Does he imagine that a tourist, who spends a couple of days or a week in a foreign country, whose language he does not speak, can make friends there?
And even if he does speak the language, making friends abroad is very difficult. I have lived in many countries as part of a Foreign Service family. Assignments were two or three years. I spoke the language of most of those countries, including French and German, and in countries with another language, it was almost always possible to find someone who could speak English, French, or German. Yet making friends, as opposed to acquaintances, was very difficult; establishing a friendship requires a significant investment of time and energy, and when it is known that you are only a temporary resident, few people are willing to make that investment. To make friends with a tourist, who arrives with a couple of thousand of his compatriots, is not going to happen.

Besides, international travel is very expensive, and many people who do travel complain about the complications and harassments of the TSA, the airlines, and an increasing number of places which no longer welcome tourists – Venice is an extreme example, but it is hardly alone. And if an American can speak the language of a foreign country, he can subscribe to magazines and newspapers, and often internet channels, from that country from the comfort of his home in the U.S.

So, Snyder’s heart is in the right place, but his head is stuck in the Ivy League aerie.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on January 26, 2021
Review Body:
I purchased this book interested in a short treatment of an important theme I am very concerned with as the Trump administration gives way to the Biden administration. I know others, Mr. Snyder, for example, were concerned in early 2017 the Trump presidency would turn tyrannical. This, of course, is always a possibility, but I did not see it and was not concerned. While the Trump presidency did provide more than enough to agitate the person already predisposed against the man, these concerns proved largely unfounded.

Reading this book now just days into the Biden administration, I am struck by how much more obviously prescient it is regarding the current state of affairs than the time for which it was written. For such a short book, it is replete with warnings that that strike at the heart of threats to our Republic that have nothing to do with Donald Trump, but with the scorned and vindictive political and media establishment hell-bent on revenge: the need for paper ballots to ensure election integrity is powerfully promoted (I wonder if this will make it into the second edition); beware the ‘one-party state’; warnings against the perversion of language; exhortations to resist words like ‘terrorism’, ‘emergency’, and ‘exception’ that would-be tyrants invoke to consolidate power; and countless denunciations of efforts to silence and eliminate opposition parties. The are even not-so-subtle allusions to the dangers of alternative media and tech tyranny (which I also suspect may be conspicuously absent from future editions).

Were the overt, anti-Trump portions of this book removed, ‘On Tyranny’ would read more like a prospective elixir to the excesses of the nascent post-Trump order than a work intended to protect us from Trump. If the author stands by his work, he may find himself in the somewhat uncomfortable position of having inadvertently written an excellent book, on accident. As a non-partisan who did not vote for Donald Trump in either 2016 or 2020, I am genuinely grateful for the accidental triumph, as the book makes some excellent points.

Review Body: I bought this book at Barnes and Noble roughly a week ago and I'm just a little more than halfway through it. A lot of the lessons that Snyder asserts are good practice for people on all sides of the political spectrum. A good example is lesson 11 which pushes the reader to investigate for themselves and learn how to discern facts. The book is filled with practical common sense lessons like this. That being said, my biggest issue with the book is the utter lack of citations. The author asserts a lot of potential facts that range from 20th century history to Trump's election with no evidence of where they got their claims. A lot of it is, of course, easily google-able but it would've helped Snyder's arguments and my fact-checking if sources were cited. This really wouldn't be too big a deal if Snyder's work wasn't so heavily biased against Trump. I understand On Tyranny was the result of the fear and uncertainty that was generated by the 2016 election, and I'm not a big Trump fan myself, but its never a good idea to make claims about someone without at least naming an article or interview to back those claims up. There's a lot in this book that, in my opinion, can genuinely help Americans to do their part in protecting our rights and freedoms, but the focus is so Trump heavy that it isn't going to age well if, in the end, it turns out Trump isn't America's Lenin or Hitler. All around the book isn't bad if you can read it without political bias

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on April 18, 2019
Review Body:
I found the 20 principles spot on, but beyond each of their first pages, it was hit or miss. The principles are ABSOLUTELY needed for everyone within the electorate across the isle. Conservatives and liberals alike must recognize tyranny in whatever form is seeps in. And believe me, it is seeping in, which is why I thought this book was timely... But in the end, this book truly only served as one purpose; a unique outlet for the author's political unrest and need to publicly air a temper tantrum. I say unique, because his rantings are cleverly folded within the instructive batter.

The author digressed often into snip-it narratives about his much despised POTUS despite the fact that at one point in his book, he renounces that very practice. I found it pseudo-intellectual especially since he leaves very few references for us to follow-up and has the reader take him at his word for his ideological apologetics (tin-foil hat firmly on head). I can't recommend this as a perennial or a modern encheridion. But I can recommend renting it from your library to at least look at the initial statements on each principle. Those are good. Many of his supporting thoughts are solid as well when they don't devolve into his political rants.

Here is my issue. The professor intelligently spins genuine history with his clever rhetoric to tell a half-story of the grave mistake of totalitarianism via his favorite despised brand, fascism. Truly, it was a nightmare and not one to be repeated. He does, however, make sure to mention the atrocities of the Soviet regime on a few spare occasions, but only in an attempt to feign balance between what the world considers the extremes of the spectrum. Pay attention and you will see how clever he is with his wording.

While he's incredibly fond of repeating "right-wing" fascism, "right-wing" totalitarianism, "right-wing" authoritarianism, he does not mention once "left-wing" anything as he is trying his hardest to correlate "right-wing" with everything evil in this world while neglecting to mention that it has in fact been "left-wing" communism that has accounted for the lion's share of genocide among the totalitarian regimes. Linen alone making Hitler look like a choir boy. Mind you, they are both totalitarian dictators. The only time he does mention "communism" is when he is passively referring to the regime. However, when he is actively referring to the atrocities of communism, he is very careful not to use the word communism and specifically opts to use the words "Soviet" and "Bolshevik" instead as not to tie the word communism too closely to its' true history. Why? Because Communism and Socialism share the same goal while they do not share the same tactic of violence. In the end, it's a failed state... It became clear half-way through the book that the author has clear Socialist sentiments. Liberal Constitutionalists take note.

At one point, I had to put the book down and laugh. Even I went to a liberal university, and my professors wouldn't have allowed me to make such blanket statements without challenging my presumptions by properly researching the opposing view point and including them parenthetically. Truly, this whole book could have be written WITHOUT the political bias. It really could have been read across the isle or strictly historical. And yet, the professor treats his audience as he treats his students and foists his opinions upon us as if everything he stamps his feet about is pure gold, manna from heaven.

At one point, he urges readers to disconnect from the internet and read the printed word; something I am HIGHLY in favor of and have found therapeutic in nursing my own intellectual wounds inflicted by the public education system. However, his reading list is uniquely socialist in nature, while containing a few gems, some of which I will certainly read.

While we're at it, if you really want to know what socialism entails, see George Bernard Shaw's (1928) tome of a book "The Intelligent Woman's Guide to Socialism and Capitalism." (No, it is not specifically feminine in nature. It was written for a specific woman upon request.) At least then you will have it out loud and clear without the added pontification (although Shaw is known to pontificate). Feel free to turn to the last page and make a decision then and there whether that's a pill you can swallow. If you're wondering why read Shaw, he was a founding member of the Fabian Socialists of England. Enough said.

I really wanted to like this book as a good portion of what he has written about his principles is actually very relevant. A good portion of what he draws out in each section is also really helpful. Yet, he makes the mistake of using this little booklet as a podium for his own political unrest. He purposefully ignores the totalitarian sentiment within the activist uprisings of the modern leftist movement; not liberalism, but leftist ideology. Again, while his recommended reading list suggests otherwise, the book itself seems classically liberal enough. Nothing to balk at unless you just can't stomach his palpable derision of the current president and his complete avoidance of the corruption within the opposing campaign. (Let's face it, American politics took a dump a long time ago when we decided to ignore the guiding Constitutional advice of our Founding Fathers.) I guess we'll see in the coming years if this president crushes the rights of women and takes voting rights away as the author suggests is clearly going to happen. I'm not holding my breath, but I'm willing to be wrong as horrible as it would be for those things to happen.

I give it a 3 because it is a quick read, the primary principles are solid and necessary, and it was inexpensive. But one thing is certain. Tyranny is not knocking on our door. It has been in our house for over 100 years. It's only been in the recent decade that the powers that be have felt it safe to turn up the heat using an un(federally)educated populace to push the needle for them. (Enter the likes of the Fabian Society and the book I mentioned above.)

For those interested to hear it from the American horse's mouth, check out Tragedy & Hope: A History of the World in Our Time by Georgetown Professor Carroll Quigley (close acquaintance with the Clintons). Make sure to get the uncensored version. Cheers!!

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on August 1, 2018
Review Body:
On Tyranny: Twenty Lessons from the Twentieth Century by Timothy Snyder

“On Tyranny” is a brief book that provides twenty keen observations on how tyranny takes hold. Author and Professor of History at Yale University, Timothy Snyder provides readers a valuable synopsis of what history has taught us about tyranny and how to avoid it. This concise 130-page book presents twenty lessons from the twentieth century.

Positives:
1. Brief with substance.
2. A fascinating topic, lessons of history regarding tyranny.
3. Timothy Snyder is a subject matter expert.
4. Much wisdom packed in one small book “Aristotle warned that inequality brought instability, while Plato believed that demagogues exploited free speech to install themselves as tyrants.” “What might seem like a gesture of pride can be a source of exclusion.”
5. Discusses the concept of anticipatory obedience. “Milgram grasped that people are remarkably receptive to new rules in a new setting. They are surprisingly willing to harm and kill others in the service of some new purpose if they are so instructed by a new authority.”
6. How are freedom can be jeopardized. “But the sense of the saying was entirely different: that human nature is such that American democracy must be defended from Americans who would exploit its freedoms to bring about its end.”
7. The reality of our current situation. “The odd American idea that giving money to political campaigns is free speech means that the very rich have far more speech, and so in effect far more voting power, than other citizens.”
8. What the Nazi regime taught us. “If lawyers had followed the norm of no execution without trial, if doctors had accepted the rule of no surgery without consent, if businessmen had endorsed the prohibition of slavery, if bureaucrats had refused to handle paperwork involving murder, then the Nazi regime would have been much harder pressed to carry out the atrocities by which we remember it.”
9. The effects of privatization. “Because the American federal government uses mercenaries in warfare and American state governments pay corporations to run prisons, the use of violence in the United States is already highly privatized.”
10. The attack on facts. “To abandon facts is to abandon freedom. If nothing is true, then no one can criticize power, because there is no basis upon which to do so. If nothing is true, then all is spectacle. The biggest wallet pays for the most blinding lights.”
11. Fascism. “Fascists despised the small truths of daily existence, loved slogans that resonated like a new religion, and preferred creative myths to history or journalism. They used new media, which at the time was radio, to create a drumbeat of propaganda that aroused feelings before people had time to ascertain facts. And now, as then, many people confused faith in a hugely flawed leader with the truth about the world we all share.”
12. Explains how resistance succeeds. “For resistance to succeed, two boundaries must be crossed. First, ideas about change must engage people of various backgrounds who do not agree about everything. Second, people must find themselves in places that are not their homes, and among groups who were not previously their friends.”
13. More lessons learned. “People who assure you that you can only gain security at the price of liberty usually want to deny you both.”
14. The need to protect our institutions. “For tyrants, the lesson of the Reichstag fire is that one moment of shock enables an eternity of submission. For us, the lesson is that our natural fear and grief must not enable the destruction of our institutions.”
15. The difference between a patriot and a nationalist. “The point is that patriotism involves serving your own country.” “The president is a nationalist, which is not at all the same thing as a patriot. A nationalist encourages us to be our worst, and then tells us that we are the best.”

Negatives:
1. A good reference summary but the topic merited a much deeper treatment.
2. Conservatives will have many issues with this book.
3. Reads more like a blog or a pamphlet than an in-depth book.
4. No supplementary material provided.
5. No links to notes.
6. No formal bibliography.

In summary, I enjoyed this brief book but the truth is this type of material required more depth. If you are looking for a brief treatment to whet your appetite this will suffice but look elsewhere for more depth. That said, there is a lot of wisdom packed in one small book. It’s worth the price of coffee so why not? Read it.

Further recommendations: “Bloodlands” by the same author, “American Fascists” by Chris Hedges, “Fascism” by Madeleine Albright, “How Democracies Die” by Steven Levitsky, “No Is Not Enough” by Naomi Klein, “Democracy in Chains” by Nancy MacLean, and “The Invention of Russia: The Rise of Putin and the Age of Fake News”.

Review Body: I found this very short book mildly informative (about 14,000 words, 30 pages of regular text, stretched to 126 pages in its pocket format). The author draws parallels between tyrannies of the past and the one Trump and his cult seek to create in the US today. That flavor is established on the first page when the authors writes, the Founders “contemplated the descent of ancient democracies and republics into oligarchy and empire. As they knew, Aristotle warned that inequality brought instability, while Plato believed that demagogues exploited free speech to install themselves as tyrants.” Given the title, parallels are drawn from Stalin, Mao, and Hitler. Occasionally I first assumed the author was listing acts of these men, only to find it was Trump. External validation proves him right. Some sections are more penetrating than others: “If nothing is true, then no one can criticize power, because there is no basis on which to do so.” Clearly what the tyrants did, and Trump hopes to do. Compared with, “Make an effort to separate yourself from the internet. Read books.” Such common sense might be a healthy prescription for the reality TV crowd, but the Amazon / Goodreads crowd won’t be that impressed.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on November 23, 2017
Review Body:
This book is a quick read. Each of the twenty lessons on how tyrants did their work in the twentieth century, and Snyder's prescriptions for resisting them, takes only a minute or two to read. Most of the most potent examples come from the tyrannies of the Axis Powers and the USSR countries in the middle of the century. To anyone well versed in those histories, there is little new here; but given the sorry state of history teaching in our schools, this is an important book of lessons.

One thing about Snyder's book is quite irritating: He illustrates most of his lessons with examples drawn from the real tyrannies of the past, then he relentlessly adds examples from the Trump Administration that he wants us to believe are equal. It gets really repetitive: this is how Hitler and Trump did this; this is how Stalin and Trump did that; this is how Fascist Italy and Trump did the other thing. When Snyder presents a lesson that would be perfectly illustrated by an example of what Obama did, somehow that is never mentioned.

Either Snyder is incredibly self-unaware, or one has to suspect that he lacks the discipline to not use this book as an anti-Trump vehicle. I still recommend the book, but Lordy, his relentless equating Trump with the worst totalitarian tyrannies of modern times is really off-putting. I have to wonder which of the two goals--teach needed lessons on tyranny, or propagandize against Trump--was uppermost in Snyder's mind.

This notion coupled with the books brevity makes this book more of an introduction to theories of thought and lessons from history - more often than not this book made me want to read the authors cited and their development of the ideas presented. In a book that is 6 inches tall and 4 incheas wide and only 126 pages, it seems appropriate that "On Tyranny" is no more than 20 lessons for us to learn form and put into practice.

Review Body: Well written though more detailed information can be had by a study of history as I have done for years and with a focus on the Republic of Weimar. Hitler was appointed chancellor of the Reichstag by a failing President Paul von Hindenburg. Author Timothy Snyder fails to make that clear and also fails to state that NAZI is an acronym for Nationalsozialismus or National Socialism. In my mind there is neither right nor left in political policies. This is two-dimensional thinking. There are policies that lead to freedom or prosperity or policies that lead to tyranny. That said, our primary focus should be on the society that produced a particular government. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is reported to have said, "If God is pleased with a community, He will put the best among them as their leader. But, if he is displeased, He will allow the worst among them to lead." We can complain and blame our government all we want but the ultimate responsibility always falls on the citizens. Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on October 2, 2017
Review Body:
I went looking for a book on the common pitfalls that democracies/republics fall into when they slip into totalitarianism. This book covers exactly that. Timothy Snyder tries to remain apolitical but it is definitely left leaning. It is interesting to compare this to a right leaning book like "The Law" by Frederick Bastiat. Or for fictional versions covering the same question there is always the Ayn Rand books. Despite the opposite polarity of those books they do make some common points. Resist a one party system, support limits on the size of government, support the rights of the individual.

Their contrasting points are interesting also. Bastiat is obsessed with taxation and colors it as unlawful theft. I suppose there exists some level of taxation where I would agree with him but to paint all taxes as plunder is too broad a brush. Ayn Rand is obsessed with Makers and Takers. She sees the rise of tyranny as the success of the Takers over the Makers. She puts the scientists, engineers and craftsmen on a pedestal and dismisses the rest of humanity and bipedal leeches. Being an engineer I find this flattering but monochromatic. Let's face it, scientists and engineers need help too. If you've ever met one you know what I'm talking about.

Snyder covers the most territory and offers not one or two root causes of tyranny but twenty. By using a finer brush he avoids some of the overstatement that I find in the other books.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on September 26, 2017
Review Body: I'm going to go a bit against the grain on this one. This book is like the Tuesdays with Morrie version of political activism. Its message boils down to this: Americans are not special; if we don't actively defend our democracy, we can fall into the same trap of authoritarianism that ensnared 20th century Europe (because apparently the lessons we can learn from the 20th century don't include the likes of Pinochet, Castro or the Khmer Rouge). Author Timothy Snyder lists 20 plans of action to "fight back" against the tide of authoritarianism, most of which are pretty vague and forgettable. While acknowledging the danger of left-wing authoritarianism, he compares most of the modern American political climate to Nazi Germany specifically. It's not that there aren't lessons to be learned there (and I highly recommend Andrew Nagorski's Hitlerland for anyone interested), but, unfortunately, that well has been a bit poisoned from rampant overuse. This book doesn't offer much substance, even taking into account its slim form. It also tips a bit into hysteria. However, it does offer some basics on political involvement and 20th century history that some people may find useful.

He then goes on and on listing Democrat talking points used against Trump, such as it's not patriotic to praise Putin or to dodge the draft or to mock disabled veterans. Yawn. It could have been more useful if instead of "freaking out" the author had provided a better step by step account of the loss of institutional independance and democracy in the historical events he refers to (essentially Nazism and communism), and how those steps came to be rationalized and eventually accepted and how they (might) compare with the current situation.

Review Date: Reviewed in the United States on September 12, 2017
Review Body:
As someone who has read a great deal about the rise of European fascism in the 20th century, I have been waiting for a serious study that would connect the dots to what is going on in the United States today. Sadly, this isn't it.

Certainly, the parallels are striking, beginning with the left/right polarization of the Weimar electorate and stalemate in the Reichstag that resulted in governance by executive decree well before Hitler assumed power; the emergence of a right wing demagogue promising to return the country to it's former glory; a constitutional system that allowed assumption of power by an individual with the support of substantially less than a majority of the electorate; the scapegoating and persecution of minorities; identification with and encouragement of ultra-nationalists defining the state and citizenship therein in racial terms; the rise and encouragement of armed militias and non-state violence to intimidate opponents of the regime; attacks on the independent press and reliance upon propaganda techniques to rewrite history and promote the views of the leader without regard to objective fact.

While Snyder touches on these themes, his use of the historical evidence, particularly in the first half of the book, lacks focus and precision, leaving the reader with the feeling that this is more of an anti-Trump screed than a serious effort at comparative analysis. If you believe that Trump is a threat to our democracy (as I do) and that the parallels to Hitler's rise to power are both instructive and frightening, then you will be dismayed that the first book to attempt the analogy has done such a poor job of it.

Even though this book was clearly an exposé on the more tyrannical tendencies of Trump, the author didn't once mention Trump's name throughout it. Instead, he would cryptically refer to him as "the president" or other such vague descriptors. This was an annoying and cowardly stylistic choice, in my opinion.

That being said, it was an easy read, and it brought up several interesting examples of tyranny from history. I especially appreciated that he held communist tyranny to the same level of scrutiny as any other form of tyranny. However, his contemporary emphasis on Trump is bound to make this a dated work in less than a decade's time. Let's just hope we won't look back at it as being prophetic.

Review Body: I was given On Tyranny by a friend, who highly recommended. And I know people who have bought several copies in order to gift them to friends and family. So perhaps my expectations were a bit high, but I ended up disappointed. The book's lessons are too short and superficially presented, and one gets the sense that the author is both talking to an audience who is near illiterate about world's history, and at the same time pursuing a simplistic, almost populist, agenda. Which is rather ironic, given that the main (never mentioned directly) target of the book is Donald Trump. And before anyone assails me, I am a card carrying liberal who thinks Trump is by far the lowest point in American politics in several generations. So, read it if you truly have no idea about history or the threat of tyranny. Otherwise look for something a bit more juicy, it shouldn't be difficult to find (e.g., stuff by my CUNY colleague Corey Robin, or Noam Chomsky, of course).
